title: Infinite Paths in Graphs: ℕ-Indexed Formalization
description: Provides the foundational definition of infinite paths in graphs for Lean 4. Defines InfiniteWalk (ℕ-indexed), IsEulerWalk (covers all edges + edge-injective), HasOneWayInfiniteEulerPath, and BiInfiniteWalk (ℤ-indexed). Shows the ℕ-indexed approach is equivalent to Stream'-based definitions. Enables the Erdős-Grünwald-Weiszfeld theorem formalization.

overview.historicalContext:
Leonhard Euler's 1736 paper 'Solutio problematis ad geometriam situs pertinentis' ('Solution of a problem relating to the geometry of position') solved the Königsberg bridge problem — can one walk through the city crossing each of its 7 bridges exactly once? Euler proved the answer is no, founding graph theory in the process. He observed that the parity of vertex degrees determines the answer: an Euler path exists iff exactly 0 or 2 vertices have odd degree. Hierholzer (1873) gave the constructive algorithm.

For infinite graphs, the question is subtler: which connected countable graphs have a one-way infinite Euler path (traversing every edge exactly once, never returning)? Erdős, Grünwald, and Weiszfeld (1936) characterized this: a connected locally finite countable graph has a one-way infinite Euler path iff (i) at most 2 vertices have odd degree, and (ii) for every finite vertex set S, the graph G−S has at most 2 infinite components. The finite-degree parity condition is necessary but no longer sufficient.

Formalizing the Erdős-Grünwald-Weiszfeld theorem in Lean 4 requires a precise definition of 'infinite path'. This file provides that foundation: the ℕ-indexed InfiniteWalk structure, which avoids coinductive complications since Stream' V = ℕ → V definitionally in Lean 4.
overview.problemStatement: Is there a clean Lean formalization of 'infinite path' (bi-infinite or one-way infinite) in a graph using Mathlib's Stream or Path API? The HasInfiniteEulerPath stub in KonigsbergOQ03.lean needs this semantic foundation.
overview.proofStrategy: Use ℕ → V instead of Stream'. The ℕ-indexed approach is definitionally equivalent but avoids coinductive reasoning: InfiniteWalk G = { vertex : ℕ → V // ∀ n, G.adj (vertex n) (vertex (n+1)) }. The Euler condition splits: 'at least once' (CoversEdge) + 'at most once' (IsEdgeInjective).
keyInsights: The key design choice: ℕ → V (functions) vs. Stream' V (codata). The ℕ-indexed approach works with standard induction and avoids the coinductive eliminator. Both are definitionally equivalent since Stream' V = ℕ → V in Lean 4's type theory.

The 'exactly once' encoding: split into (a) CoversEdge = at least once, (b) IsEdgeInjective = at most once. This decomposition avoids the ∃! n quantifier which requires decidability in some contexts. Both halves of the conjunction are classical Prop.

SameEdge handles undirected edges: step m and step n traverse the same edge if (vertex m = vertex n ∧ vertex (m+1) = vertex (n+1)) OR (vertex m = vertex (n+1) ∧ vertex (m+1) = vertex n). No Sym2 needed.

BiInfiniteWalk uses ℤ → V for Erdős-Grünwald-Weiszfeld: some formulations require a bi-infinite path starting at -∞. The structure mirrors InfiniteWalk but with ℤ indexing and Int.add for the step condition.

The InfiniteGraph structure is deliberately self-contained (not importing KonigsbergOQ03.InfiniteGraph) to avoid transitive dependency on a file with pre-existing compilation issues — an application of the 'islands of correctness' pattern: reproduce the minimal interface locally rather than waiting for an upstream fix, then bridge later.

sections.title: Part 0: Infinite Graph Definition
sections.summary: Self-contained InfiniteGraph: adj predicate, symmetry, loopless.
sections.mathContext: A simple infinite graph $G = (V, \sim)$ where $\sim : V \to V \to \text{Prop}$ is irreflexive ($\neg(v \sim v)$, `loopless`) and symmetric ($u \sim v \Rightarrow v \sim u$, `symm`). No finiteness hypothesis on $V$.

sections.title: Part 1: One-Way Infinite Walks
sections.summary: InfiniteWalk structure: vertex : ℕ → V, step_adj. stepPair, sameEdge (undirected edge equality).
sections.mathContext: An infinite walk: $w = (v_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ with $v_n \sim v_{n+1}$ for all $n$. Two steps $m, n$ traverse the same undirected edge iff $(v_m = v_n \wedge v_{m+1} = v_{n+1}) \vee (v_m = v_{n+1} \wedge v_{m+1} = v_n)$.

sections.title: Part 2: Euler Walk Conditions
sections.mathContext: Euler walk: covers all edges (surjective: $\forall u \sim v,\, \exists n,\, w.\text{sameEdge with } (u,v)$) and traverses each at most once (injective: $m \neq n \Rightarrow \neg w.\text{sameEdge}(m, n)$). Formally: $\text{IsEulerWalk}(w) = \text{CoversEdge}(w) \wedge \text{IsEdgeInjective}(w)$.

sections.title: Part 3: Bi-Infinite Walks
sections.mathContext: A bi-infinite walk: $(v_n)_{n \in \mathbb{Z}}$ with $v_n \sim v_{n+1}$ for all $n \in \mathbb{Z}$. Erdős-Grünwald-Weiszfeld: a connected locally finite countable graph has a bi-infinite Euler path iff every vertex has even degree.

sections.title: Part 4: Basic Properties
sections.summary: step_is_adj, step_ne (endpoints distinct), covers/injective projections, ofStream (Stream' equivalence).
sections.mathContext: Looplessness gives $v_n \neq v_{n+1}$: from `step_adj n : G.adj (v_n) (v_{n+1})`, substituting `h : v_n = v_{n+1}` yields `G.adj (v_n) (v_n)`, contradicting `G.loopless`. Stream' equivalence: `Stream' V` is defined as `ℕ → V`, so `ofStream s h = \{vertex := s, step_adj := h\}` is the identity at type level.

conclusion.summary: The ℕ-indexed InfiniteWalk provides a clean, sorry-free foundation for infinite Euler paths in Lean 4. The definitions are ready for use in the Erdős-Grünwald-Weiszfeld theorem formalization. Key simplifications: ℕ over Stream', split Euler condition, undirected edges via sameEdge without Sym2.
openQuestions: Prove the Erdős-Grünwald-Weiszfeld theorem: G has a one-way Euler path iff (1) at most 2 vertices of odd degree and (2) every finite subgraph has even edge parity. This is the main application of these definitions.
Connect InfiniteWalk to Mathlib's SimpleGraph.Walk API: is there a coercion or embedding from finite Walk to InfiniteWalk (by appending a trivial 'tail')?
